ei.subject: 영어1
ei.title: Keré's Architecture and the Serpentine Pavilion

fullPassage:
Keré tackled the problem of limited resources during the building's construction by using materials that were easy to find in the region in the same manner as before. First of all, he built the walls of the building using bricks made from readily available stone in the region. These bricks help cool the building by absorbing intense daytime heat and later releasing it during the night.

As with many other buildings, an overhanging roof protects the brick walls from the harsh African sun while also facilitating air circulation below. To capture fresh air and let hot air escape, Keré also added wind towers on top of each classroom. The school is surrounded by a screen made from fast-growing local eucalyptus trees. This screen provides more than just protection against dust and wind. It also creates casual spaces where students can gather as they wait for their classes to begin.

Serpentine Pavilion
Over time Keré's work has expanded well beyond Africa. It now includes temporary and permanent structures in Denmark, Germany, Italy, Switzerland, the UK, and the USA. Perhaps not too surprisingly, his works outside of Africa are influenced by his experiences in Gando. A perfect example is the colorful Serpentine Pavilion in London. Since the year 2000, the Serpentine Gallery in the UK has annually invited distinguished architects from around the world to design a pavilion, which provides a place of rest for visitors. In 2017, the honor was extended to Keré. Drawing inspiration from his hometown, where locals would gather to work, converse, and study beneath the shade of trees, he modeled his design after a large tree. The pavilion's roof, resembling the wide branches of a tree, includes a transparent layer that allows sunlight to spread into the pavilion below. Visitors may enter the pavilion through one of its four entrances and sit around the central ring to look up at the sky.

The pavilion's exterior walls, shaped like triangles and made of blue wooden blocks, reflect Keré's cultural heritage. In his hometown, residents traditionally wear blue clothing during times of celebration, and the triangles symbolize luck and confidence. Holes carved in the walls let in light to promote an airy, bright atmosphere, and a gap between the roof and walls ensures a lot of air circulation. The roof's unique funnel design channels rainwater toward the building's center. During rainfall, the water gathers and pours down like a waterfall. It is then sent through a drainage system for the purpose of watering plants. This method of rainwater collection stands as Keré's symbolic message about the global challenges of water scarcity and climate change.

Keré believes that architecture is primarily a service to humanity and hopes that his projects will inspire people "to dream of better." The more his vision is shared with a wider audience, the better our world will become.

questions.passage: Keré tackled the problem of limited resources during the building's construction by using materials that were easy to find in the region in the same manner as before. He built the walls of the building using bricks made from (A)[readily / rarely] available stone in the region. These bricks help cool the building by absorbing (B)[intense / gentle] daytime heat and later (C)[releasing / absorbing] it during the night. As with many other buildings, an overhanging roof protects the brick walls from the harsh African sun while also facilitating air circulation below. To capture fresh air and let hot air escape, Keré also added wind towers on top of each classroom. The school is surrounded by a screen made from fast-growing local eucalyptus trees.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 (A), (B), (C)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것끼리 짝지은 것은?

det.korean: 쉽게(readily) 구할 수 있는 돌. 강렬한(intense) 낮 열기. 밤에 방출(releasing).
det.analysis:
✅ ① readily–intense–releasing: 벽돌이 쉽게 구할 수 있는 돌로 만들어지고, 강렬한 열을 흡수해 밤에 방출. 원문 일치.
❌ ② absorbing은 낮에 흡수하는 것이지 밤에 하는 것이 아님
❌ ③ rarely(드물게)는 readily(쉽게)의 반의어, gentle(부드러운)은 intense(강렬한)의 반의어
❌ ④ 전부 부적합
det.tip: readily(쉽게) ↔ rarely(드물게) / intense(강렬한) ↔ gentle(부드러운) / absorb(흡수) ↔ release(방출)

The pavilion's roof includes a (B)[transparent / opaque] layer that allows sunlight to spread into the pavilion below. questions.stem: 다음 글의 (A), (B), (C)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것끼리 짝지은 것은?

det.korean: 저명한(distinguished) 건축가들. 투명한(transparent) 층. 배수(drainage) 시스템.
det.analysis:
✅ ③ distinguished–transparent–drainage: 모두 원문 적합.
❌ ① symbolic system은 drainage system이 원문
❌ ② anonymous(익명의)는 distinguished(저명한)의 반의어
❌ ④ anonymous가 부적합
det.tip: distinguished(저명한) ↔ anonymous(익명의) / transparent(투명한) ↔ opaque(불투명한) / drainage system = 배수 시스템

questions.stem: 다음 글의 (A), (B), (C)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것끼리 짝지은 것은?

det.korean: 넓은 가지를 닮은(resembling) 지붕. 축하(celebration) 때 파란 옷. 물 부족(scarcity)의 도전.
det.analysis:
✅ ② resembling–celebration–scarcity: 모두 원문 적합.
❌ ① heritage(유산)는 times of celebration이 원문
❌ ③ abundance(풍부)는 scarcity(부족)의 반의어
❌ ④ 전부 부적합. imitating(모방)은 resembling(닮은)과 유사하나 원문은 resembling
det.tip: resemble(닮다) vs imitate(모방하다) — 지붕이 나뭇가지를 '닮았다'는 외형적 유사성 / scarcity(부족) ↔ abundance(풍부)

questions.stem: 밑줄 친 낱말 중 문맥상 부적절한 것은?

det.korean: ④ hindering(방해하는) → 원문: facilitating(촉진하는). 지붕이 공기 순환을 촉진한다.
det.analysis:
✅ 정답 ④: hindering(방해하는)은 facilitating(촉진하는)의 반의어.
❌ ① limited(제한된) 원문 적합
❌ ② available(이용 가능한) 원문 적합
❌ ③ protects(보호하다) 원문 적합
det.tip: facilitate(촉진하다) ↔ hinder(방해하다). 지붕이 태양으로부터 보호 + 공기 순환 촉진 = 이중 기능.

questions.stem: 밑줄 친 낱말 중 문맥상 부적절한 것은?

det.korean: ② shrunk(줄어든) → 원문: expanded(확장된). 작업 범위가 아프리카를 훨씬 넘어 확장됨.

❌ ③ permanent(영구적인) 원문 적합
❌ ④ surprisingly(놀랍게도) 원문 적합
det.tip: expand(확장하다) ↔ shrink(줄어들다). 아프리카를 넘어 덴마크, 독일, 이탈리아 등으로 확장.

questions.stem: 밑줄 친 낱말 중 문맥상 부적절한 것은?

det.korean: ③ congestion(혼잡, 정체) → 원문: circulation(순환). 지붕과 벽 사이 틈이 공기 순환을 보장한다.
det.analysis:
✅ 정답 ③: congestion(혼잡, 정체)은 circulation(순환)과 의미가 반대. 공기가 정체되는 것이 아니라 순환되어야 함.
❌ ① converse(대화하다) 원문 적합
❌ ② reflect(반영하다) 원문 적합
❌ ④ funnel(깔때기) 원문 적합
det.tip: circulation(순환) ↔ congestion(혼잡, 정체). air circulation = 공기 순환 / traffic congestion = 교통 정체

As with many other buildings, an overhanging roof protects the brick walls from the harsh African sun while also facilitating air circulation below. To capture fresh air and let hot air escape, Keré also added wind towers on top of each classroom. The school is surrounded by a screen made from fast-growing local eucalyptus trees. This screen provides more than just protection against dust and wind. It also creates casual spaces where students can gather as they wait for their classes to begin.

Serpentine Pavilion
Over time Keré's work has expanded well beyond Africa. It now includes temporary and permanent structures in Denmark, Germany, Italy, Switzerland, the UK, and the USA. Perhaps not too surprisingly, his works outside of Africa are influenced by his experiences in Gando. A perfect example is the colorful Serpentine Pavilion in London. Since the year 2000, the Serpentine Gallery in the UK has annually invited distinguished architects from around the world to design a pavilion, which provides a place of rest for visitors. In 2017, the honor was extended to Keré. Drawing inspiration from his hometown, where locals would gather to work, converse, and study beneath the shade of trees, he modeled his design after a large tree. The pavilion's roof, resembling the wide branches of a tree, includes a transparent layer that allows sunlight to spread into the pavilion below. Visitors may enter the pavilion through one of its four entrances and sit around the central ring to look up at the sky.

The pavilion's exterior walls, shaped like triangles and made of blue wooden blocks, reflect Keré's cultural heritage. In his hometown, residents traditionally wear blue clothing during times of celebration, and the triangles symbolize luck and confidence. Holes carved in the walls let in light to promote an airy, bright atmosphere, and a gap between the roof and walls ensures a lot of air circulation. The roof's unique funnel design channels rainwater toward the building's center. During rainfall, the water gathers and pours down like a waterfall. It is then sent through a drainage system for the purpose of watering plants. This method of rainwater collection stands as Keré's symbolic message about the global challenges of water scarcity and climate change.

Keré believes that architecture is primarily a service to humanity and hopes that his projects will <u>inspire</u> people "to dream of better." The more his vision is shared with a wider audience, the better our world will become.
